points.title: Linear and nonlinear texts
points.brief: A linear text such as a novel is read in order from start to end. A nonlinear text such as a website or interactive story lets the reader choose a path, which changes how meaning is built.

points.title: Frame and parallel narratives
points.brief: A frame narrative places one story inside another. Parallel narratives run two story lines side by side. Both create layers of meaning as the stories comment on each other.

points.title: Ethical dilemmas in texts
points.brief: Many texts present problems with no simple right answer, where a character must choose between two goods or two harms. Readers weigh both sides rather than judging quickly.

points.title: Justifying a personal response
points.brief: A strong personal response explains why a text affected you by pointing to how it was made, such as its tone, a character's voice or the genre, not only to how you felt.

points.title: Language and identity online
points.brief: The way people speak shows who they are and which groups they belong to. Online platforms create new words and ways of speaking that signal identity.

points.title: Representation as construction
points.brief: Every text is a construction. Its composer chooses what to include and leave out, shaped by their context, their creative aims and assumptions they may not notice.

points.title: Using and subverting conventions
points.brief: Texts can follow the conventions of their form, adapt them or subvert them, deliberately breaking an expected pattern to surprise the audience or make a point.

points.title: Nonfiction that tells a story
points.brief: Some nonfiction, such as memoir and feature journalism, uses fiction techniques like scene, dialogue and character to engage readers while staying true to fact.

points.title: Metafiction
points.brief: Metafiction is writing that draws attention to itself as a text, such as a narrator who speaks to the reader about how the story is being told.

points.title: Extended metaphor
points.brief: A metaphor developed across a paragraph, poem or whole text, so that one comparison shapes the reader's understanding of a complex idea.

points.title: Juxtaposition and contrast
points.brief: Placing two different things side by side, such as wealth and poverty in one scene, so each makes the other stand out and an idea becomes clear.

points.title: Pathetic fallacy
points.brief: Using weather or nature to reflect a character's feelings, such as a storm building as an argument grows, so emotion is shown without being stated.

points.title: Verbal, situational and dramatic irony
points.brief: Verbal irony says the opposite of what is meant. Situational irony is an outcome opposite to what was expected. Dramatic irony is when the audience knows something a character does not.

points.title: Country in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander writing
points.brief: Many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander writers use imagery, symbol and metaphor drawn from Country and Place to express culture, identity and belonging. Teach reading these respectfully.

points.title: Omniscient and limited narration
points.brief: An omniscient narrator knows every character's thoughts. A limited narrator stays close to one. Narrative distance is how near the telling sits to a character's mind.

points.title: Unreliable narrators
points.brief: An unreliable narrator cannot be fully trusted, because they lie, misunderstand or are biased. Readers notice gaps between what the narrator says and what the details show.

points.title: Multiple narrators
points.brief: Some texts are told by several narrators in turn. Each gives a partial view, and the reader builds a fuller picture by comparing them.

points.title: Author and persona
points.brief: The real author is different from the voice in the text. A poem's speaker or a story's narrator is a persona, so analysis says the speaker feels, not the poet feels.

points.title: Direct, indirect and free indirect speech
points.brief: Direct speech quotes a character's words, indirect speech reports them, and free indirect speech blends a character's thoughts into the narrator's voice without quotation marks.

points.title: Foil characters
points.brief: A foil is a character whose qualities contrast with another's, such as a careless friend beside a cautious hero, so the main character's traits stand out.

points.title: Internal and external conflict
points.brief: External conflict is a struggle against another person, society or nature. Internal conflict is a struggle within a character's mind. Characters drive the plot through both.

points.title: Characters and values
points.brief: Characters can reflect the values of their world, challenge them or subvert them. What happens to a character can suggest what the text approves of or questions.

points.title: Building character through narration
points.brief: Characters can be shaped indirectly by who focalises the story and how their words are reported, not only by description and dialogue.

points.title: Beginning in the middle
points.brief: Starting in the middle of the action, known as in medias res, skips or delays the orientation so a reader is pulled straight in and fills in the background later.

points.title: Nonlinear structure
points.brief: Flashbacks, time jumps and stories told out of order control what a reader knows and when, which builds suspense or changes how events are judged.

points.title: Narrative and identity
points.brief: Narratives can show and shape personal and shared identities. Writers from different cultures, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander writers, choose how to represent their own experiences.

points.title: Themes that unify a text
points.brief: A theme can hold a text together, so that its characters, settings and images all feed one central idea. Showing how several parts of a text work towards the same theme.

points.title: Readers and their contexts
points.brief: Readers bring their own time, culture and experience to a text, so different audiences can find different themes and meanings in the same work.

points.title: Reading through a lens
points.brief: A text can be read from a particular perspective, such as gender, class or culture, which brings some ideas forward. Different readings can each be supported with evidence.

points.title: The composer's context
points.brief: An author's personal, cultural and political context can shape their perspective, the ideas they represent and the form they choose.

points.title: Affirming and challenging values
points.brief: A text can support the attitudes of its time or push against them. Comparing a text's values with those of its context shows which it does.

points.title: Language and cultural knowledge
points.brief: Words from a particular language can carry cultural knowledge and ways of seeing. Writers who use Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Languages or Aboriginal English in texts pass on meaning that English alone may not hold.

points.title: Blending subjective and objective voice
points.brief: Writers move between an objective voice that presents evidence and a subjective voice that gives opinion, choosing each for effect in an argument.

points.title: Satire and parody
points.brief: Satire uses humour, irony and exaggeration to criticise people or ideas. Parody imitates a text's style to mock it or make a point.

points.title: Logical fallacies
points.brief: Weak arguments such as attacking the person, the false choice between only two options and the slippery slope. Spotting them makes it easier to judge an argument and avoid them in your own.

points.title: Questioning a text's authority
points.brief: A text's authority is not fixed. Readers test it by checking its sources and comparing it with other texts, and a second text can challenge the claims of the first.

points.title: Authority in interactive texts
points.brief: In games, social media and other interactive texts, users and algorithms help shape what is shown, so control over meaning is shared between the maker and the audience.

points.title: Style and purpose
points.brief: A text's style, its word choice, sentence patterns, imagery and form, is shaped by its purpose and in turn shapes how the reader responds.

points.title: A signature style
points.brief: Some writers and film directors have a style recognisable across their works, through repeated subjects, structures, images or techniques.

points.title: Literary movements
points.brief: Groups of texts from one period share a style, such as Romantic poetry with its focus on nature, emotion and the individual, or Gothic fiction with its dark settings and dread.

points.title: Genre and values
points.brief: The conventions of a genre carry values, such as who gets to be the hero. Noticing them shows what a text assumes about the world.

points.title: How genres change
points.brief: Genres change over time. They are adapted, mixed into hybrids and subverted as audiences and values change, which shows in remakes and new versions of old stories.

points.title: Retelling a classic
points.brief: A modern retelling keeps parts of an older story and changes others for a new audience. Judging a retelling means asking what it kept, what it changed and why.

points.title: Connections between texts
points.brief: Reading texts against each other, through shared themes, forms or references, can deepen understanding of both and of the culture they come from.

points.title: How a text's reputation changes
points.brief: A text can be praised or criticised when it first appears and judged differently later, as readers' values and contexts change.

points.title: Varying sentence length
points.brief: Mixing long and short sentences controls pace. A run of short sentences builds tension, and a long one can slow the reader down for detail or reflection.

points.title: Subject-verb agreement
points.brief: A verb must agree with its subject, even when the subject is a collective noun such as team or a long noun group such as the list of names on the wall.

points.title: Choosing the passive voice
points.brief: Writers choose the passive voice on purpose, to put the focus on what happened, to sound impersonal in a report, or to leave out who was responsible.

points.title: Punctuation for effect
points.brief: A colon can set up a reveal, a semicolon can balance two ideas, and an ellipsis can show a pause or a thought left unfinished. Each changes how a reader moves through a sentence.

points.title: Greek and Latin roots
points.brief: Many English words are built on Greek and Latin roots, such as graph (write) and port (carry). Knowing the root helps spell a word and work out its meaning.

points.title: Choosing words for tone
points.brief: Words with similar meanings carry different connotations, so choosing scolded or criticised or attacked changes the tone and how the reader judges a moment.

points.title: Technical vocabulary and register
points.brief: Each subject and form has its own vocabulary. Using the right technical terms, at the right level of formality, makes writing precise and credible.

points.title: Connectives that show relationships
points.brief: Connectives show how ideas relate, such as however for contrast, therefore for cause and effect, for example for illustration, and moreover for adding weight.

points.title: A strong thesis
points.brief: A thesis answers the question with an arguable position, not a fact or a summary, and sets up the points the essay will develop.

points.title: Sustaining an argument
points.brief: Each body paragraph opens with a topic sentence that links to the thesis, so the argument builds from one paragraph to the next.

points.title: Analysing evidence
points.brief: Strong analysis names the technique, gives a short example, then explains its effect and how it supports the argument. Explaining how, not just what, is the difference.

points.title: Discursive writing
points.brief: A discursive text explores an idea from several angles without needing to win an argument, often moving from a personal experience to a wider reflection.

points.title: Writing from research
points.brief: Informative writing gathers facts from reliable sources, organises them under clear headings or topic sentences, and says where information came from.

points.title: Camera shots
points.brief: Long shots show setting, mid shots show a character's body language and close-ups show emotion or a telling detail. Each guides what the viewer notices.

points.title: Camera angles
points.brief: A high angle looks down on a subject and can make it seem weak. A low angle looks up and can make it seem powerful. An eye-level shot feels neutral.

points.title: Mise-en-scène and lighting
points.brief: Mise-en-scène is everything placed in the frame, the setting, props, costume and actors' positions. Lighting, such as harsh shadows or soft light, sets the mood.

points.title: Sound and editing in film
points.brief: Diegetic sound comes from the world of the film and non-diegetic sound, such as a score, is added over it. Editing pace, from slow cuts to quick ones, controls tension.

points.title: The sonnet and other fixed forms
points.brief: A sonnet has 14 lines with a set rhyme pattern and often a turn in its argument. Fixed forms give shape to an idea, while free verse follows no set pattern.

points.title: Rhythm, metre and enjambment
points.brief: Metre is the regular pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables. Enjambment runs a sentence over a line break, which can build pace or create surprise.

points.title: Conventions of drama
points.brief: A soliloquy shares a character's thoughts alone on stage, an aside is spoken to the audience unheard by others, and stage directions guide how a play is performed.

points.title: Delivering a speech
points.brief: Intonation, emphasis, pause and pace, with signposting phrases such as firstly and finally, help an audience follow and remember a spoken argument.

points.title: Judging sources
points.brief: A reliable source has a clear author with expertise, a recent date, a purpose that is not only to sell or persuade, and claims that other sources support.

points.title: Revising for a reader
points.brief: Rereading a draft as the audience would, to find what is unclear, what needs evidence and what can be cut, before polishing the language.

points.title: Reflecting on your own style
points.brief: Noticing the choices you make as a writer, what works and what you repeat, and setting a goal to try a new technique or form.
